newsitem.title: KENYA: FEATURE-Kenya tensions find scant outlet in politics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Kenya tensions find scant outlet in politics.

text.p: President Daniel arap Moi, one of Africa's longest-serving rulers, has a firm grip on Kenya's levers of power and faces no electoral threat from a divided opposition despite rising social tension.
Political analysts say he and the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) are bound to win elections set for some time later this year.
"There is absolutely no alternative to a win for Moi and for KANU. The way it is now, KANU has already won," said Peter Warutere, managing editor of the Economic Review, a leading Nairobi weekly.

But opinions vary on whether Moi's political dominance will ensure stability -- the government says its economic reforms are on course to help lift Kenyans out of poverty, while the opposition warns of impending mayhem.
Social tensions are high with the government admitting much poverty and Kenya regularly pilloried abroad for abuse of human rights and rampant official corruption.
Four student activists have been killed, at least three by police, since last December.

The landless, people afflicted by drought, a surging number of urban street children and students with diminishing prospects of employment are all groups whose discontent has found no expression in conventional politics.
For opposition supporters and many independent political observers in Kenya, the electoral playing field is so uneven that truly free and fair polls are impossible.

Western diplomats say that KANU has an unfair advantage in the drawing of boundaries, the national electoral commission, voter registration and access to state radio -- the crucial medium for 30 million Kenyans.
Given the rules of the game, even opposition strategists appear ready to throw in the towel, months before the polls.
"If we have the same rules as 1992 then Moi will be declared the winner," said accountant David Kabeberi, an adviser to Kenneth Matiba, chairman of the Ford-Asili opposition party.
MOI IS KENYA'S ROBUST VETERAN
If these predictions are borne out, Kenya will start the 21st century with a president who entered parliament in 1955 and has been at the summit of the state since 1967.
Moi, now aged 72 and in robust form, was vice-president for 11 years before inheriting the presidency in 1978 from Jomo Kenyatta, father of the former British colony's independence.
Moi has already declared he will run in the next elections for what will be his final five-year presidential mandate under the current constitutional rules.
The elections have to be held this year. Moi can choose the date but most analysts interviewed by Reuters expected the presidential and parliamentary polls to be at the end of 1997.
The disarray in the opposition, which is split on tribal and personal grounds, will give Moi the chance to partially erase the bitter memory of 1992.

In Kenya's first multi-party polls, he came first with only 35 percent of the presidential vote, a very low score for an incumbent in Africa. Had he been forced into a second round run-off against Matiba, the odds were stacked against him.
Moi's KANU just kept control of the 200-seat parliament thanks to favourable constituency boundaries and 12 members nominated by the president.
The political passions of 1992 have subsided, deflated by the opposition's inability to unite and by the easing of pressure on Moi by Western nations about human rights.
OPPOSITION WARNS OF POSSIBLE CHAOS

Moi is philosophically opposed to multi-partyism in Africa, warning that it deepens tribal divisions. His opponents accuse the president of making his own pessimistic predictions come true by favouring his Kalenjin minority.
"The multi-party system was a vain hope for people who thought things would get better, but they haven't. I see a situation where chaos and mayhem is not to be ruled out," said Kabeberi.

The government can point to steady economic reforms since 1993 which have virtually met the key conditions of donors. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by a disappointing 4.8 percent in 1996 but many domestic and foreign investors feel safer with a Moi presidency and anticipate quick privatisation of inefficient state utilities after the elections.

"What (foreign investors) see is a huge market with no competition. The country is stable enough for long enough to exploit that opportunity. The government is not going to change for the next five years," said a foreign businesswoman.
"We have no doubts that we will win the forthcoming general elections," said KANU's secretary-general, Joseph Kamotho, the education minister.
"The man (Moi) is still so energetic, so resourceful, any criticism just because he is over 70 does not hold water."
He rejected accusations that KANU played an unfair political game.
"I don't think KANU has taken an advantage of being in power. If the opposition was in power maybe they would be worse," Kamotho said.

The loaded dice and the prospect of defeat may persuade some of the main opposition leaders to boycott the polls. Even without a boycott, turnout could be low in 1997 because of widespread disillusionment and apathy.
"There is no point participating in an election that you know will be rigged," said Ford-Asili's Kabeberi, stressing that his party had not taken a decision to boycott.
"If there was a fair election there is no way Moi or the ruling party would be elected," he said. But he added: "There is no chance that the rules will be changed".
